parts.overview: The brain is the central processing organ of the nervous system. The cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum work together to coordinate conscious experience and essential body functions.
parts.function: Integrates sensation, plans and controls movement, supports learning and memory, and regulates autonomic and endocrine activity.
parts.location: Inside the cranial cavity, protected by the skull, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.
parts.bloodSupply: Internal carotid and vertebral arteries contribute to the cerebral circulation. Their branches communicate around the base of the brain in the arterial circle.
parts.innervation: Neural pathways connect brain regions with the spinal cord and cranial nerves. Brain tissue itself lacks the pain receptors found in surrounding meninges and vessels.
clinicalNotes: Different cerebral regions support different functions; lesion location matters as well as lesion size.
The atlas illustrates a reference surface and does not show an individual patient or every internal brain structure.

quiz.question: Which structure is especially important for coordination and balance?
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum helps coordinate movement, timing and balance.

quiz.q: Where is the brain located?
quiz.question: Where is the brain located?
quiz.explanation: The brain lies within the cranial cavity and is protected by the skull and meninges.

parts.overview: The heart is a muscular pump with two atria and two ventricles. Its right and left sides move blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations respectively.
parts.function: Generates the pressure needed to circulate blood. Valves promote one-way flow, while the conduction system coordinates contractions.
parts.location: In the middle mediastinum within the pericardium, between the lungs. Most of its mass lies to the left of the midline.
parts.bloodSupply: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta. Most cardiac venous blood returns through the coronary sinus to the right atrium.
parts.innervation: Sympathetic cardiac nerves and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve influence rate and conduction. Specialized cardiac cells generate the normal rhythm.
clinicalNotes: Myocardial oxygen delivery depends on coronary circulation; coronary obstruction can injure cardiac muscle.
Heart valves have distinct positions and auscultation areas. A schematic body location is not an auscultation guide.

quiz.question: Which chamber normally pumps blood into the aorta?
quiz.explanation: The left ventricle ejects blood into the aorta for systemic circulation.

quiz.question: The coronary arteries supply which tissue?
quiz.explanation: Coronary arteries supply the myocardium with oxygenated blood.

parts.overview: The paired lungs contain branching airways and alveoli. The right lung usually has three lobes; the left has two and a cardiac notch.
parts.function: Provide a large surface for exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.
parts.location: Within the right and left pleural cavities of the thorax, on either side of the mediastinum and above the diaphragm.
parts.bloodSupply: Pulmonary arteries carry blood for gas exchange; pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium. Bronchial arteries supply supporting lung tissues.
parts.innervation: Pulmonary plexuses carry vagal parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers that influence airway smooth muscle and glands.
clinicalNotes: The pleura and pressure relationships in the thorax are important for ventilation.
A surface mesh cannot display alveolar microstructure or establish respiratory disease.

quiz.question: How many lobes does the right lung usually have?
quiz.explanation: The right lung usually has upper, middle and lower lobes.

quiz.q: Where does most gas exchange occur?
quiz.question: Where does most gas exchange occur?
quiz.explanation: Thin alveolar walls and surrounding capillaries support gas exchange.

parts.overview: The liver is a large gland with important metabolic, synthetic and digestive roles. Its tissue is arranged around an extensive vascular network.
parts.function: Produces bile, processes absorbed nutrients, synthesizes many plasma proteins, stores selected nutrients and participates in metabolism of numerous substances.
parts.location: Mainly in the right upper abdomen beneath the diaphragm, extending into the epigastric region.
parts.bloodSupply: Receives blood from the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein. Hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava.
parts.innervation: Autonomic fibers reach the liver through the hepatic plexus, including sympathetic and vagal parasympathetic pathways.
clinicalNotes: Portal blood brings absorbed materials from the digestive tract to the liver.
The liver has several segmental descriptions; the introductory mesh does not identify a surgical resection plane.

quiz.question: Which vein delivers much of the absorbed nutrient-rich blood to the liver?
quiz.explanation: The hepatic portal vein brings blood from much of the digestive tract to the liver.

quiz.q: Which digestive fluid is produced by the liver?
quiz.question: Which digestive fluid is produced by the liver?
quiz.explanation: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

parts.overview: The stomach is a distensible muscular organ between the esophagus and duodenum. Its regions include the cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part.
parts.function: Stores a meal temporarily, mixes it into chyme, secretes acid and digestive enzymes, and produces intrinsic factor needed for vitamin B12 absorption.
parts.location: Mainly in the left upper abdomen and epigastrium. Shape and position vary with filling and body habitus.
parts.bloodSupply: Branches of the celiac arterial system supply the stomach, including gastric, gastro-omental and short gastric arteries. Venous drainage enters the portal system.
parts.innervation: Vagal parasympathetic pathways, sympathetic fibers through the celiac plexus and the enteric nervous system regulate activity.
clinicalNotes: The gastric mucosal barrier helps protect tissue from acid and digestive enzymes.
Stomach position changes with filling; the body illustration is an approximate location.

quiz.question: The stomach empties directly into which structure?
quiz.explanation: The pyloric outlet of the stomach opens into the duodenum.

quiz.q: Intrinsic factor is important for absorption of which vitamin?
quiz.question: Intrinsic factor is important for absorption of which vitamin?
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 and supports its absorption in the terminal ileum.

parts.overview: The small intestine consists of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. Folds, villi and microvilli greatly increase its absorptive surface.
parts.function: Completes much of chemical digestion and absorbs most nutrients into blood or lymph.
parts.location: Extends from the stomach to the ileocecal junction. The jejunum and ileum form mobile loops in the abdominal cavity.
parts.bloodSupply: The duodenum receives pancreaticoduodenal branches from celiac and superior mesenteric territories. Jejunal and ileal branches arise from the superior mesenteric artery.
parts.innervation: Enteric circuits coordinate local activity, modified by vagal parasympathetic and sympathetic pathways.
clinicalNotes: The terminal ileum has a particular role in uptake of bile salts and vitamin B12.
A surface atlas does not show the microscopic absorptive structures.

quiz.question: Which is the correct proximal-to-distal order?
quiz.explanation: From the stomach, contents pass through the duodenum, then jejunum, then ileum.

quiz.q: Villi mainly increase which property?
quiz.question: Villi mainly increase which property?
quiz.explanation: Villi increase the surface available for intestinal absorption.

parts.overview: The pancreas contains exocrine acini and endocrine islets. Its head, neck, body and tail extend across the upper abdomen.
parts.function: Delivers digestive enzymes and bicarbonate to the duodenum. Islet hormones, including insulin and glucagon, help regulate blood glucose.
parts.location: Mostly retroperitoneal, posterior to the stomach. The head lies within the duodenal curve and the tail approaches the spleen.
parts.bloodSupply: Pancreaticoduodenal arteries supply much of the head. Pancreatic branches of the splenic artery supply much of the body and tail.
parts.innervation: Vagal parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers reach the pancreas through abdominal autonomic plexuses.
clinicalNotes: The pancreatic duct and biliary pathways have a close anatomical relationship near the duodenum.
Exocrine and endocrine functions belong to different cellular components within the same organ.

quiz.question: Which pancreatic component releases insulin?

quiz.question: Most of the pancreas lies in which position?
quiz.explanation: Most of the pancreas is retroperitoneal, behind the stomach.

parts.overview: The gallbladder is a small hollow organ connected to the biliary ducts by the cystic duct.
parts.function: Stores and concentrates bile between meals, then releases it into the biliary pathway.
parts.location: In a fossa on the inferior surface of the liver in the right upper abdomen.
parts.bloodSupply: Usually supplied by the cystic artery, commonly a branch of the right hepatic artery. Vascular patterns vary.
parts.innervation: Autonomic fibers arrive through the celiac and hepatic plexuses, with vagal parasympathetic contributions.
clinicalNotes: Biliary anatomy and arterial branching show clinically important variations.
Gallstones are solid material within the biliary system; a reference mesh is not a way to detect them.

quiz.question: The gallbladder mainly stores which substance?

quiz.question: Which duct connects the gallbladder to the biliary tree?
quiz.explanation: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder with the common hepatic duct pathway.

parts.overview: The paired kidneys contain cortex and medulla organized around a collecting system. Nephrons are their functional filtration and processing units.
parts.function: Form urine, regulate fluid and electrolyte balance, contribute to acid-base control, and produce hormones involved in blood pressure and red cell production.
parts.location: Retroperitoneal on either side of the vertebral column. The right kidney is usually slightly lower than the left.
parts.bloodSupply: Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta. Renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava.
parts.innervation: The renal plexus carries predominantly sympathetic fibers that influence renal vascular tone and other functions.
clinicalNotes: Renal filtration depends on specialized microanatomy that is not visible in a surface model.
The renal hilum transmits vessels, nerves and the pelvis of the collecting system.

quiz.question: What is the functional unit of the kidney?

parts.overview: The urinary bladder is a distensible hollow organ with a muscular wall. Ureters enter it, and the urethra carries urine away.
parts.function: Stores urine and participates in coordinated emptying through contraction of the detrusor and control of the outlet.
parts.location: In the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis when relatively empty. A full bladder extends upward into the lower abdomen.
parts.bloodSupply: Vesical branches of the internal iliac arterial system supply the bladder; the exact pattern differs between individuals.
parts.innervation: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic pathways support detrusor contraction. Sympathetic and somatic pathways participate in storage and outlet control.
clinicalNotes: Bladder size and position change substantially as it fills.
Storage and emptying depend on coordinated neural pathways as well as bladder muscle.

quiz.question: Which muscle forms much of the bladder wall?

quiz.question: Which tubes carry urine from kidneys to bladder?
quiz.explanation: Ureters convey urine to the bladder; the urethra carries it outward.

parts.overview: The spleen is a lymphoid organ with red pulp and white pulp. It monitors blood rather than filtering lymph.
parts.function: Participates in immune responses to blood-borne material, removes aging blood cells and helps recycle their components.
parts.location: In the left upper abdomen, adjacent to the stomach and below the diaphragm.
parts.bloodSupply: The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk. The splenic vein contributes to formation of the hepatic portal vein.
parts.innervation: Autonomic fibers reach the spleen through the splenic plexus and are predominantly sympathetic.
clinicalNotes: The spleen has a close relationship with the lower left ribs and adjacent abdominal organs.
A person can survive without a spleen, but splenic immune functions remain important.

parts.overview: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ with lobules containing a cortex and medulla. It is most prominent earlier in life.
parts.function: Provides the environment for development and selection of T lymphocytes.
parts.location: Mainly in the anterior superior mediastinum, sometimes extending into the lower neck.
parts.bloodSupply: Branches from nearby thoracic and cervical arteries, including internal thoracic and inferior thyroid vessels, contribute to its supply.
parts.innervation: Autonomic fibers accompany vessels; immune and endocrine signals are central to thymic function.
clinicalNotes: Thymic tissue normally undergoes age-related involution and increasing fatty replacement.
The reference adult mesh does not represent the typical thymus of every age group.

quiz.question: The thymus is classified as what?

parts.overview: The pituitary has anterior and posterior components with different developmental origins and functions. It is closely connected to the hypothalamus.
parts.function: The anterior pituitary secretes hormones affecting several endocrine organs. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone made by hypothalamic neurons.
parts.location: In the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica at the base of the skull, connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.
parts.bloodSupply: Hypophyseal arteries supply the gland. A portal vascular system carries hypothalamic regulatory signals to the anterior pituitary.
parts.innervation: Hypothalamic axons extend into the posterior pituitary. Anterior pituitary activity is largely regulated by hormones arriving through portal vessels.
clinicalNotes: The nearby optic chiasm is an important anatomical relationship.
The anterior and posterior components should not be treated as functionally interchangeable.

quiz.question: The pituitary sits in which bony feature?

quiz.explanation: ADH is synthesized in hypothalamic neurons and transported to the posterior pituitary.

parts.overview: Each adrenal gland has an outer cortex and an inner medulla. These regions produce different groups of hormones.
parts.function: The cortex produces steroid hormones, including cortisol and aldosterone. The medulla releases catecholamines during sympathetic activation.
parts.location: Retroperitoneal, near the superior poles of the kidneys. The glands have their own capsules and vascular supply.
parts.bloodSupply: Superior, middle and inferior suprarenal arterial groups arise from different sources. Each gland usually drains through a major suprarenal vein.
parts.innervation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly stimulate adrenal medullary chromaffin cells.
clinicalNotes: Cortex and medulla differ in tissue origin and regulation.
The right and left suprarenal veins have different usual drainage pathways.

quiz.question: Chromaffin cells belong to which region?
quiz.explanation: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla release catecholamines.

parts.overview: The femur is the long bone of the thigh. Its head, neck, trochanters, shaft and distal condyles provide articulation and muscle attachment.
parts.function: Transfers load between hip and knee and acts as a lever for lower-limb movement.
parts.location: Between the hip and knee. Its head articulates with the acetabulum, and its distal end participates in the knee joint.
parts.bloodSupply: The proximal femur receives important branches from circumflex femoral vessels; nutrient and periosteal vessels supply the shaft and other regions.
parts.innervation: Periosteal and vascular-associated nerves include sensory and autonomic fibers. Nearby joint innervation arises from several lower-limb nerves.
clinicalNotes: Femoral head blood supply is an important anatomical consideration after a femoral neck fracture.
The supplied atlas model is a right femur, centered for viewing.

parts.overview: Biceps brachii is a two-headed muscle in the anterior compartment of the arm. Its long and short heads join into a common muscle belly.
parts.function: Supinates the forearm and flexes the elbow. It also contributes to shoulder movement and stability.
parts.location: Anterior arm, extending from scapular origins to an insertion on the radius and an aponeurotic expansion.
parts.bloodSupply: Muscular branches of the brachial artery supply much of the muscle.
parts.innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve, mainly through C5 and C6 spinal segments.
clinicalNotes: Biceps is a forearm supinator as well as an elbow flexor.
The supplied geometry represents the long and short heads on the right side.

parts.overview: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped musculotendinous partition between thorax and abdomen. A central tendon connects its muscular portions.
parts.function: The principal muscle of inspiration. Contraction increases thoracic volume and contributes to abdominal pressure changes.
parts.location: Forms the inferior boundary of the thoracic cavity. Its major openings transmit the vena cava, esophagus and aorta through or behind it.
parts.bloodSupply: Several vessels contribute, including inferior phrenic, superior phrenic, pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries.
parts.innervation: Motor supply is through the phrenic nerves, from C3 to C5. Sensory supply includes phrenic and peripheral lower intercostal pathways.
clinicalNotes: The diaphragm moves during breathing; the mesh is a static reference shape.
Phrenic nerve function is essential to normal diaphragmatic contraction.

parts.overview: The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system. Ascending and descending pathways connect it to the brain, and segmental circuits support reflexes.
parts.function: Transmits sensory and motor information and integrates many reflex and autonomic activities.
parts.location: Within the vertebral canal. In adults it usually ends near the L1-L2 vertebral level, with nerve roots continuing below.
parts.bloodSupply: Anterior and posterior spinal arteries are reinforced by segmental vascular contributions.
parts.innervation: Spinal nerve roots connect the cord to peripheral nerves. Gray matter contains neuronal circuits, while white matter contains long pathways.
clinicalNotes: The adult spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral canal; cord segments and vertebral levels are not identical.
The cauda equina consists of nerve roots below the usual end of the cord.

parts.overview: Skin consists of epidermis and dermis, with a subcutaneous layer beneath. The epidermis forms a renewing outer barrier.
parts.function: Protects the body, contributes to temperature control, supports sensation and helps initiate vitamin D synthesis.
parts.location: Covers the external body surface. Its thickness and appendages vary across regions.
parts.bloodSupply: Vessels in the dermis and underlying tissues supply the skin. The epidermis is avascular and receives nutrients by diffusion.
parts.innervation: Cutaneous sensory endings detect touch, temperature and other stimuli. Autonomic fibers influence glands and small vessels.
clinicalNotes: Skin depth matters when describing an injury; the epidermis and dermis differ structurally.
The illustration is a simplified cross-section, not a histological specimen. No licensed 3D skin model is bundled.

quiz.explanation: The epidermis contains no blood vessels and is nourished by diffusion from deeper tissues.

quiz.question: Which is a major function of skin?
quiz.explanation: Skin provides a protective barrier and also supports sensation and temperature regulation.

parts.overview: The paired testes contain seminiferous tubules and interstitial tissue. Germ cells, supporting cells and hormone-producing cells have distinct roles.
parts.function: Produce sperm in the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone mainly from interstitial Leydig cells.
parts.location: Within the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity, with vascular and duct connections through the spermatic cords.
parts.bloodSupply: Testicular arteries usually arise from the abdominal aorta. The pampiniform venous plexuses contribute to heat exchange and venous return.
parts.innervation: Autonomic fibers reach the testes through the testicular plexuses accompanying their vessels.
clinicalNotes: Scrotal position and vascular heat exchange support the temperature requirements of spermatogenesis.
This entry reflects the male reference dataset. The introductory catalog is not a complete reproductive anatomy atlas.
